clue.text: Composer of largely 26 piece giving one for nothing

indicators.note: one (the letter I) is given in exchange for nothing (the letter O), so the O of the piece is swapped out

parts.note: 26 across is BRISKET; most of it is BRISK, and a brisk musical piece or movement is an allegro

explanation.surface: A composer is described by part of a piece of music, with a trade of one thing for nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Largely 26' is BRISK(ET), and the Italian tempo mark for brisk names the piece. 'Giving one for nothing' swaps its final O for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Gregorio Allegri was the Italian Baroque composer famous for his setting of the Miserere.

clue.text: Father of James, fantastic help down under

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or wild, so the letters are made into a new form

parts.note: down under is Australia, abbreviated AUS

explanation.surface: James's father is given fantastic help in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic' shuffles HELP together with AUS. In the Bible, James the Less is called the son of Alphaeus.
explanation.definitionFit: Alphaeus, also spelt Alpheus, is named in the New Testament as the father of the apostle James the Less.

clue.text: He brought about a row — old cricketer

indicators.note: brought about means turned round, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old cricketer caused a row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought about' rearranges A ROW and OLD. Larwood was at the centre of the 1932-33 Bodyline row, so the surface is true.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Larwood was an English fast bowler of the 1920s and 1930s.

clue.text: Weapon turned, for example, on the filth

parts.note: a gun is a weapon

indicators.note: turned means the abbreviation is reversed

explanation.surface: A weapon is turned on the police, slangily called the filth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The filth' looks like British slang for the police, but the definition is just muck. 'Turned' reverses EG to GE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunge is a British word for sticky, unpleasant matter or muck.

clue.text: I'm put out over the concert being unrehearsed

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go over, that is around, the concert
put out means disturbed, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the Proms are the famous summer concerts in London, and a prom is a promenade concert

explanation.surface: Someone is put out because the concert was performed without rehearsal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' looks like annoyance, but only 'out' signals the rearrangement; 'over' wraps it round the concert, the Proms being London's famous summer concert series.
explanation.definitionFit: An impromptu performance is done without preparation or rehearsal.

clue.text: One to sort out what's for lunch …

indicators.note: out signals that the letters of 'one' and 'to sort' are put out of order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone is setting out to sort out the lunch menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges I (one) and TO SORT together into the Italian rice dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A risotto is an Italian rice dish, a typical thing to eat at lunchtime.

clue.text: Ways to address an African explorer?

indicators.note: to address someone is to speak to them, so the name is taken as spoken

parts.note: Cecil Rhodes was a British imperialist who opened up southern Africa

explanation.surface: A question about how one should formally address an explorer of Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ways to address' looks like forms of address, but 'Ways' is the definition and the explorer's name is said out.
explanation.definitionFit: Roads are ways from one place to another.

clue.text: Carteret's misplaced desire?

indicators.note: misplaced letters are put in the wrong positions, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Carteret has a desire that has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Misplaced' rearranges CARTERETS. The definition alludes to Tennessee Williams's play A Streetcar Named Desire.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tennessee Williams's play the streetcar is named Desire, so the desire is a tram.

clue.text: American stool gets volunteers to drill on time

parts.note: the TA, the Territorial Army, is Britain's volunteer reserve force
to bore is to drill a hole

explanation.surface: An American stool gets volunteers drilling on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: A taboret is a low stool or small table, the term being chiefly American.

clue.text: Bunting turns up a lot in some ornamentation

indicators.note: the reversed letters go in the shortened word
some means only part of the word is used, its opening letters
in a down clue turning up means reading the words backwards

explanation.surface: Bunting is hung up with plenty of other decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bunting' suggests flags, but it is a bird. 'Some' shortens ornamentation to ORN; 'turns up' reverses A LOT to TOLA, and 'in' places it inside ORN.
explanation.definitionFit: The ortolan is a small European bunting, eaten as a delicacy.

clue.text: … what's proverbial for the course, bargain vegetable

parts.note: the proverb says something expected is 'par for the course'
a snip is a British word for a bargain, something very cheap

explanation.surface: A continuation of the lunch theme: the expected dish for the course is a cheap vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links to 5 across, so 'course' reads as a course of a meal, but it is the golf course of the idiom. SNIP is British slang for a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: The parsnip is a pale root vegetable related to the carrot.

clue.text: Gymnastic type rocking boat with wrecked car

indicators.note: a wrecked car is smashed up, so its letters are jumbled
a rocking boat is shaken about, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An agile person is on a rocking boat with a wrecked car.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word has its own anagram signal: 'wrecked' turns CAR into ACR and 'rocking' turns BOAT into OBAT.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrobat performs gymnastic feats such as tumbling and balancing.

clue.text: llustrious Cockney's gone off the Guardian for rousing desire

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the H at the start of a word

parts.note: an illustrious person is a hero, a celebrated figure

indicators.note: gone off means spoiled, so the letters of 'gone' are jumbled

parts.note: the newspaper speaking of itself says 'us'

explanation.surface: A famous Londoner has walked away from the newspaper for an arousing reason.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held drops the I of 'Illustrious'. A Cockney says 'ERO for HERO; 'off' turns GONE into GENO, and the Guardian, where the puzzle appeared, refers to itself as US.
explanation.definitionFit: Erogenous means sensitive to sexual stimulation, so arousing desire.

clue.text: Join up space with nothing separating sides

parts.note: an en is a printer's unit of space

indicators.note: the nothing comes between the two sides and so separates them

parts.note: the two sides are right and left, R and L
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: An instruction to join up a space with nothing in between its edges.
explanation.walkthrough: EN is a printer's space; 'separating' puts O between R and L, the right and left sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up or enlist, as in joining a course or the army.

clue.text: Old city, about what's as good as a wink

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the phrase is read backwards

parts.words: what's as good as a wink
parts.note: the saying runs 'a nod is as good as a wink', so the thing that is as good is 'nod is'

explanation.surface: An ancient city is described with reference to a knowing gesture.
explanation.walkthrough: From the saying 'a nod is as good as a wink', the words NOD IS are reversed by 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidon was an ancient Phoenician port city, now Saida in Lebanon.

clue.text: Race that's wearing on participants

indicators.note: the letters of 'wearing on' all take part, rearranged, in making the race

explanation.surface: A race that wears down those who take part in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' reads as a contest, but it is a nation or people. The anagram signal is loose: 'participants' has the letters of WEARING ON taking part in a new arrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Race here means a people or nation, and Norwegians are the people of Norway.

clue.text: University cost including number and weight

indicators.note: the price takes the number inside it

parts.note: the price of something is its cost
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Fees at a university involve calculating numbers and weights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Including' is the container signal: the number sits inside the cost, and the weight follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Princeton is an Ivy League university in New Jersey.

clue.text: What can't be described or sworn at?

definitions.text: What can't be described or sworn at?

parts.words: What can't be described or sworn at?
parts.note: something beyond words; jokily, eff as in 'effing and blinding' means to swear

explanation.surface: A question about what lies beyond both description and cursing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ineffable means too great or extreme to be expressed in words.

clue.text: Bring in a foreign female to go on the game

parts.note: to import is to bring goods in from abroad
une is the French for 'a' before a feminine noun

explanation.surface: Someone brings in a woman from abroad to work as a prostitute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go on the game' is British slang for working as a prostitute; UNE is the French feminine 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Importune can mean solicit for immoral purposes, which is what a prostitute does when working.

clue.text: Gordius is old hat — there's no getting out of it

definitions.text: there's no getting out of it

parts.note: Gordius, the setter, says of himself 'I am', shortened to I'm
something old hat is passé, out of date

explanation.surface: The setter admits he is out of date and stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordius is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Gordius is' becomes I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: An impasse is a deadlock or dead end from which there is no way out.

clue.text: Times of hypochondria and ravishment?

parts.note: a hypochondriac is forever taking pills, so the pill stands for hypochondria
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Periods of imagined illness are compared with a violent plundering.
explanation.walkthrough: The parts come in answer order through 'of': an age of the pill.
explanation.definitionFit: Pillage is plunder and violent seizure, and ravishment in its old sense means carrying off by force.

clue.text: Monies for treasurer shortly to collect

indicators.note: to collect is to gather together, so the remaining letters are gathered into a new order
shortly means the word is cut short, keeping only its first part

explanation.surface: Money is handed to the treasurer, who will soon collect it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' trims 'treasurer' to the common abbreviation TREAS, and 'to collect' gathers those letters into RATES.
explanation.definitionFit: Rates are local property taxes in Britain, sums of money paid to the council.

clue.text: Apprentice carried it about as stock-in-trade

indicators.note: carried goes about, that is around, the learner

parts.note: took means carried
an apprentice is a learner, L as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: An apprentice carried his kit about as the tools of his trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the container signal: the learner sits inside 'carried', and 'it' is used as written. L for learner comes from the British L-plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A toolkit is the set of tools a tradesman relies on, his stock-in-trade.

clue.text: Marxist character part portrays hysteria

indicators.note: part means only part of the words is used, a run of letters within them

explanation.surface: A Marxist character part shows a fit of hysteria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marxist' suggests politics, but it means the Marx Brothers: Groucho often played crooked lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: Groucho Marx played shady lawyers, such as J. Cheever Loophole in At the Circus.

clue.text: Purse changes hands for a bean

indicators.note: the right hand, R, is changed for the left hand, L

explanation.surface: A purse passes from one person to another in exchange for a bean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changes hands' swaps R (right) for L (left) in PURSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are edible seeds of legumes, so a bean is an example of a pulse.

clue.text: Concerned with odour from somewhat antiquated works

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of the word is used, its last letter cut

parts.note: something antiquated is old
a works is a factory

explanation.surface: Smells are coming from a rather old industrial plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' signals a cut: only part of the word for antiquated is used, its final letter dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Olfactory means relating to the sense of smell.

clue.text: Sarkozy's gold sea creature

parts.note: Nicolas Sarkozy was French president, and the French for gold is or
continuing in French, mer is the sea

explanation.surface: The French president's gold is a sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarkozy signals French for both pieces. OR is also heraldic gold.
explanation.definitionFit: An ormer is an edible sea snail, the abalone, found around the Channel Islands.

clue.text: Cleft feature on point

parts.note: the chin is a facial feature
E for east is a compass point

explanation.surface: A cleft chin is a feature resting on a point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleft' looks like the dimpled chin, but the definition is a ravine. A chine is a steep cleft in cliffs, a word used on the Isle of Wight and in Dorset.
explanation.definitionFit: A chine is a deep narrow ravine cut through cliffs on the south coast of England.

clue.text: Must aid be needed to build Olympic venue?

indicators.note: building from the letters of 'must aid' constructs a new word from them

explanation.surface: A question of whether help is needed to construct an arena for the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To build' rearranges the letters of MUST AID.
explanation.definitionFit: A stadium is a large sports arena of the kind built to host the Olympic Games.

clue.text: Butcher's cut puts hazard in hazard

indicators.note: the first hazard is placed in the second

parts.note: to hazard money is to bet it, and a bet is a hazard
a hazard is a risk

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut puts one danger inside another.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word gives two different synonyms: RISK goes 'in' BET.
explanation.definitionFit: Brisket is a cut of beef from the breast of the animal.

clue.text: Henry's wife, the queen, slim and round in the middle

indicators.note: slim and round go in the middle of the queen

parts.note: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword queen
lean means slim
a round shape is like the letter O

explanation.surface: Henry's wife was a slim queen who became round around the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle' puts LEAN and O between E and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Aquitaine was the wife of King Henry II of England.

clue.text: Old prince caught replacing article from 27

indicators.note: the caught letters take the place of the article within 27

parts.note: 27 across is ELEANOR
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An old prince replaced the article from an earlier entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Replacing' puts CT, for caught, where the article AN stood in ELEANOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An elector was a German prince entitled to vote in choosing the Holy Roman Emperor.
